strengths: CityLens addresses a relevant problem with useful breadth: 11 socioeconomic prediction tasks, six domains, imagery from 17 cities, and evaluation of 17 vision-language models.

The three evaluation paradigms distinguish direct numerical prediction, normalized estimation, and supervised regression on interpretable visual attributes. Table 1 provides a useful comparison of feature extraction across models.
The city-level analysis and experiments varying satellite input and street-view image count offer useful preliminary diagnostics. The appendix documents indicator sources and representative prompts.
weaknesses: Result reporting is incomplete and potentially biased. Section 3.3.1 explicitly excludes results when either R² is at most 0.5, contradicting Figure 4, which displays many lower scores. Even if the intended threshold was −0.5, excluding poor results would obscure precisely the failures this benchmark should measure. Complete model-by-task tables, refusal rates, and explicit handling of invalid outputs are needed.

Geographic generalization is not established. The five-fold evaluation does not specify spatial blocking, grouping of overlapping imagery, or held-out cities/countries. Spatial autocorrelation and shared geographic labels could inflate performance. Moreover, several domains cover only US or UK cities, so the overall 17-city coverage does not imply broad geographic coverage for every task.

Essential baselines are missing, including conventional visual features with the same LASSO regressor, pretrained image embeddings, relevant urban prediction methods, and city-mean or coordinate-based predictors. Consequently, the experiments do not establish the value added by vision-language models. Comparing supervised feature regression against zero-shot prediction also confounds representation quality with access to labeled training data, although the discussion acknowledges this difference.

Normalized estimation is insufficiently defined. The paper does not specify the transformation, its geographic scope, or how models learn the numerical meaning of the endpoints. Table 4 merely requests a score between 0.0 and 9.9, leaving calibration ambiguous. Figure 7, labeled as normalized estimation, instead requests a proportion between 0 and 1. Poor performance therefore cannot confidently be attributed to deficient socioeconomic reasoning.

Dataset validity and harmonization need stronger documentation. Imagery dates, alignment with indicator years, spatial aggregation, and cross-country house-price comparability are unclear. Mapping ZIP-code house prices onto census tracts does not create tract-resolution observations and may introduce shared labels across folds. Several targets are themselves modeled estimates, requiring discussion of their uncertainty and potential dependence on visual or geographic predictors.

Reproducibility and statistical support are inadequate. LASSO tuning, feature scaling, fold construction, inference settings, normalization formulas, and complete task prompts are not provided. Table 1 reports standard deviations across tasks rather than uncertainty over repeated evaluations. Narrow ablations on individual models and tasks cannot support general conclusions about satellite usefulness or model scaling.

The benchmark needs a substantive treatment of responsible use and data governance. Inferring neighborhood mental health, crime, and education from appearance can reinforce stereotypes and mislead policy decisions. The manuscript does not adequately discuss ecological inference, reporting biases in labels, privacy safeguards, or redistribution rights for the collected imagery.

strengths: CityLens addresses a relevant problem and assembles a potentially useful benchmark spanning 17 cities, 11 indicators, six domains, and both satellite and street view imagery.

Evaluating 17 vision-language models provides useful breadth. The results reveal substantial differences across indicators, with stronger performance on building height and transport than on several health and crime outcomes.
The manuscript documents indicator sources, supplies representative prompts, and includes exploratory analyses of geographic variation, satellite inputs, and street view image quantity.
weaknesses: The reporting of direct and normalized prediction results is seriously problematic. Section 3.3.1 states that results with either R² ≤ 0.5 are excluded, yet Figure 4 displays many such results. This may be a missing minus sign, but excluding poor results even at −0.5 would bias the comparison. Complete model-by-task results, refusal rates, and explicit failure-handling rules are needed.

Essential baselines are missing: conventional visual features, pretrained image embeddings with the same regression head, relevant urban prediction methods such as UrbanCLIP/UrbanVLP, and city/location-only predictors. Consequently, the experiments do not establish the value of using vision-language models or distinguish model limitations from limitations of the chosen 13-feature representation.

The main paradigm comparison confounds supervision and representation. Feature-Based Regression receives task labels through LASSO training, whereas direct and normalized prediction are zero-shot; the input modalities also differ. Although the discussion acknowledges the supervision difference, superior regression performance does not establish that these models are intrinsically better feature extractors than numerical predictors.

Geographic generalization is not convincingly evaluated. Five-fold cross-validation is reported without specifying spatial separation, and there are no held-out-city or held-out-country experiments. Nearby regions, shared ZIP-derived house-price labels, and city-level differences could inflate pooled performance. City-specific scores alone do not demonstrate transfer.

Normalized estimation is insufficiently defined. The paper does not specify the normalization formula, reference population, or how models learn the meaning of the 0–9.9 scale. Figure 7, labeled as normalized estimation, instead requests a raw bachelor ratio between 0 and 1. Without consistent calibration and prompts, poor performance cannot be attributed confidently to deficient socioeconomic reasoning.

Benchmark construction and reproducibility need substantially more detail: imagery dates and alignment with target years, spatial aggregation of raster labels, harmonization of house prices across countries, fold assignments, LASSO tuning, inference settings, and the nRMSE definition. Several targets are modeled estimates rather than direct observations, but their uncertainty is not examined. The supplied manuscript also provides no usable resource link.

The analysis overstates its evidence. Table 1 reports variation across tasks rather than uncertainty across runs or folds, leaving model-ranking claims unsupported statistically. Satellite ablation covers only one model and three tasks, and image-count analysis covers one model-task pair. Explanations involving architecture, city structure, or cultural context remain speculative.

The paper lacks a substantive treatment of the risks of inferring crime, mental health, and socioeconomic status from neighborhood appearance. Geographic and subgroup bias, ecological inference errors, potential stigmatization, and imagery redistribution permissions warrant explicit discussion, particularly given the proposed policy applications.

strengths: CityLens addresses a relevant application with a useful breadth of imagery, geographic coverage, and targets: 17 cities, 11 indicators, and six domains. Consolidating these heterogeneous sources could provide a valuable research resource.

Evaluating 17 vision-language models across direct prediction, normalized estimation, and feature-based regression provides substantial descriptive coverage. Table 1 offers a useful starting point for comparing models as structured visual feature extractors.

The city-level analysis and image-input ablations investigate practical questions, and the paper openly reports weak performance on several indicators rather than presenting socioeconomic inference as solved.
weaknesses: The reporting of direct and normalized prediction is incomplete and internally inconsistent. Section 3.3.1 states that results with either R² ≤ 0.5 are excluded, yet Figure 4 contains many such results. Even if the intended threshold was −0.5, excluding poor outcomes biases comparisons and conceals important benchmark failures. Complete model-by-task results, refusal rates, and explicit failure-handling rules are needed.

Normalized estimation is insufficiently defined. The paper does not specify the normalization formula, reference population, or how models learn the scale anchors. Table 4 merely requests a score from 0.0 to 9.9, while Figure 7, labeled as a normalized example, requests the original bachelor ratio between 0 and 1. Consequently, differences between paradigms could reflect ambiguous prompting rather than numerical or geographic reasoning.

The validation does not establish geographic generalization. Five-fold cross-validation is described without specifying spatial blocking, city holdouts, or grouping of regions sharing source labels. Nearby regions and census tracts assigned values from the same ZIP code could appear across folds. City-level performance analysis is not a substitute for evaluating transfer to unseen cities.

Essential baselines are missing: conventional visual encoders or segmentation features with the same regressor, relevant urban representation methods such as UrbanCLIP/UrbanVLP, and simple city/location-based predictors. Without these comparisons, the added value of vision-language models remains unclear. Moreover, supervised LASSO versus zero-shot numerical prediction does not isolate the benefit of the feature-based formulation, although the discussion acknowledges the supervision difference.

Dataset validity and reproducibility need stronger documentation. Imagery acquisition dates, temporal alignment with labels, spatial aggregation rules, cross-country house-price harmonization, and uncertainty in modeled global indicators are not adequately specified. Reproducibility is also limited by missing split identifiers, LASSO tuning details, decoding settings, and an accessible release link in the submitted manuscript.

Several conclusions exceed the experimental support. Satellite-image utility is tested with one model on three tasks, and image-count effects with one model on one task. No repeated-run or fold-level uncertainty is reported; Table 1's SD measures variation across tasks, not statistical reliability. The appendix's claim that feature-based regression consistently outperforms direct prediction is also contradicted by points below the diagonal in Figure 9.

The benchmark lacks a substantive discussion of responsible use and data governance. Predicting neighborhood crime, mental health, and education from appearance creates concrete risks of stigmatization and ecological misinterpretation. Geographic coverage biases, limitations of administrative labels, and redistribution permissions for commercial imagery should be documented.

strengths: CityLens addresses a relevant evaluation gap: predicting regional socioeconomic indicators from urban imagery. Its coverage of 17 cities, 11 indicators, and multiple image sources provides a potentially useful resource.

The experimental effort is substantial, including 17 LVLMs, two domain-specific baselines, three prediction paradigms, and additional studies of prompting, image quantity, vision encoders, nonlinear regressors, and fine-tuning.

The results provide useful evidence that performance depends strongly on the indicator and that domain-specific training can help. UrbanVLP’s advantage over generic LVLM feature extraction is an informative finding.
The Mapillary alternative improves accessibility. The ethics statement appropriately acknowledges geographic underrepresentation and discourages operational use in sensitive settings.
weaknesses: The geographic evaluation does not establish transfer to unseen regions. Five-fold cross-validation is specified without explaining spatial blocking, city grouping, or protection against nearby samples and shared source-label units crossing folds. City-specific GDP results do not substitute for held-out-city evaluation. Spatially blocked and leave-one-city-out experiments are needed to support generalization claims.

Normalized Metric Estimation is insufficiently defined. The paper does not specify the transformation, its reference population, or how normalization parameters are estimated. The prompts request a score between 0.0 and 9.9 without explaining its quantitative anchors. Consequently, poor R² may reflect an undefined calibration task rather than deficient socioeconomic understanding; normalization also does not inherently turn R² into a ranking metric.

Reporting of direct and normalized prediction is incomplete and selectively filtered. Section 3.2 removes model-task pairs with R² ≤ −0.5 under either setting and hides model identities, without providing a complete unfiltered results table. Refusal rates and the treatment of invalid outputs are unspecified despite documented refusals. This prevents reliable model comparison and assessment of failure frequency.

Label validity and comparability need stronger justification. Appendix A.5.2 averages population raster values although the task asks for total population. ZIP-level house values assigned to census tracts are proxies rather than independent tract-level ground truth. Cross-country house-price units, currency harmonization, and imagery–label temporal alignment are not adequately documented. These issues can materially affect both task meaning and measured performance.

The comparison between paradigms confounds representation quality with access to supervision: feature-based regression trains on target labels, whereas direct and normalized prediction are zero-shot. Restricting LVLM representations to 13 predefined attributes also limits conclusions about their broader capabilities. Matched-supervision comparisons, frozen visual-embedding baselines, and city/location-only predictors are needed to isolate visual information and calibration effects.

Experimental reproducibility and statistical support are insufficient. LASSO tuning, fold construction, decoding settings, and baseline training procedures are not adequately specified. The fine-tuning study lacks training-set sizes, optimization details, and a clear account of geographic separation from evaluation data. Table 1’s SD measures variation across tasks, not uncertainty across runs; the ablations provide no confidence intervals supporting small performance differences.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Preliminary fine-tuning results are achievable performance points, not an upper bound. Explanations involving urban structure, model reasoning, and the mental-health effects of waterfront proximity are not experimentally validated. The geographic bias audit covers only GDP and does not separate model bias from label quality, imagery coverage, and target-distribution differences. These limitations weaken the diagnostic conclusions that constitute much of the paper’s contribution.

strengths: CityLens addresses a relevant benchmark gap by assembling satellite and street-view imagery for 11 socioeconomic indicators across 17 cities and evaluating 17 LVLMs.

The experimental coverage is substantial: it includes UrbanCLIP and UrbanVLP baselines, modality and image-count ablations, reasoning comparisons, nonlinear regressors, and preliminary supervised fine-tuning.
The Mapillary alternative improves accessibility. The paper also explicitly discusses geographic imbalance, privacy, and restrictions on consequential deployment.
Several findings are useful starting points, including the strong performance of UrbanVLP relative to generic LVLM feature extraction and improvements from task-specific fine-tuning.
weaknesses: The normalized prediction task is insufficiently defined. Section 2.2 specifies a 0–9.9 target range, but does not establish the normalization formula, reference population, or how models learn the scale’s endpoints. The shown prompts provide no quantitative anchors. Poor R² therefore cannot cleanly distinguish weak socioeconomic understanding from an undefined calibration problem; rank-based metrics would help test the claimed ordinal capability.

Geographic generalization is not convincingly evaluated. Five-fold cross-validation is reported without specifying spatial blocking or city-held-out splits. Nearby regions, shared street-view panoramas, and census tracts assigned overlapping ZIP-level labels could introduce dependence across folds. City-level performance comparisons do not establish transfer to unseen cities, and quantitative city-only or coordinate-based baselines are missing.

The comparison between paradigms confounds representation quality with access to supervision: feature-based regression trains a LASSO on target labels, whereas direct and normalized prediction are zero-shot. Appendix A.2 acknowledges this, but the paper still draws broad conclusions about feature extraction being preferable. The fixed 13-attribute bottleneck also limits what poor performance can establish about LVLM capabilities generally.

Reporting of direct and normalized results is incomplete and selectively filtered. Section 3.2 removes every model-task pair with R² ≤ −0.5 in either setting and hides model identities, without providing a complete numerical results table or systematic refusal statistics. Moreover, the claim that feature-based regression consistently outperforms direct prediction is contradicted by Llama4-Maverick’s house-price R² of 0.795 in Figure 7a versus 0.233 in Table 1.

Target construction needs stronger validation. Appendix A.5.2 averages raster population counts despite prompts requesting total population, and the paper does not adequately document temporal alignment between imagery and indicators or harmonization of house-price units across countries. Several labels are themselves modeled estimates, but their uncertainty and implications for benchmark validity are not examined.

Important reproducibility and uncertainty details are missing: fold construction, preprocessing and regressor tuning, generation settings, invalid-output handling, and fine-tuning dataset sizes and hyperparameters. Table 1’s SD measures variation across tasks rather than uncertainty across runs or folds, so small model differences are not supported statistically. Fine-tuning results are promising but do not constitute an upper bound.

The benchmark’s breadth exceeds the strength of its validated conclusions. Most sensitive indicators cover only the US or UK; explanations of architectural effects, geographic disparities, and mental-health reasoning are largely speculative. Although the collection effort is valuable, the unresolved evaluation and target-definition issues prevent the submission from meeting a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: CityLens addresses a relevant evaluation gap: predicting regional socioeconomic indicators from urban imagery. Its coverage of 17 cities, 11 indicators, six domains, and 17 LVLMs represents substantial dataset construction and benchmarking effort.

The experiments explore several useful dimensions, including direct prediction, normalized estimation, feature-based regression, input modalities, image quantity, reasoning prompts, vision encoders, and supervised fine-tuning.
Comparisons with UrbanCLIP and UrbanVLP provide domain-specific reference points. The appendix adds nonlinear regressors and caption embeddings, going beyond a single prediction pipeline.
The Mapillary alternative is a valuable response to proprietary imagery restrictions. The ethics statement also explicitly addresses geographic imbalance, privacy, and inappropriate operational use.
weaknesses: Normalized estimation is insufficiently defined to support the central comparison. The paper does not specify the normalization transformation, its reference population, or how its parameters are obtained. The prompts request a score from 0.0 to 9.9 without explaining what those values mean relative to the ground-truth distribution. Consequently, poor R² may reflect an undefined calibration problem rather than deficient socioeconomic understanding; R² also does not directly test the claimed relative-ranking capability.

The evaluation does not establish geographic generalization or isolate visual information from geographic priors. Five-fold cross-validation is reported without specifying spatial grouping, and no held-out-city evaluation is provided. Nearby regions and shared source labels could make ordinary folds optimistic. City-mean and coordinate-based regression baselines, together with matched image-free controls, are needed; one model's refusal in the house-price experiment does not resolve this issue.

Label validity and harmonization need substantially more scrutiny. Appendix A.5.2 averages population raster values, while the task asks for total population. ZIP-level house prices are assigned to census tracts, introducing shared, coarse labels. The manuscript does not adequately document imagery–label temporal alignment or currency and valuation-unit harmonization across countries. Several targets are themselves modeled estimates, but their uncertainty is not incorporated into the evaluation.

Reporting of direct and normalized prediction is incomplete and selectively filtered. Section 3.2 removes model–task pairs whenever either R² is at most −0.5 and hides model identities; a complete numerical results table is not supplied. Refusal rates and handling of invalid outputs are also unspecified. These omissions prevent reliable model comparisons and can distort conclusions about which estimation strategy works best.

Some conclusions exceed what the experimental design establishes. Feature-based regression receives supervised target calibration, whereas the initial direct and normalized methods are zero-shot; their performance difference cannot isolate an intrinsic advantage of feature extraction. Restricting representations to 13 predefined attributes also limits conclusions about LVLM capabilities generally. Preliminary fine-tuning results demonstrate achievable performance, not an upper bound.

Reproducibility and statistical support remain insufficient despite the breadth of experiments. Fine-tuning sample counts, training configuration, split construction, regression tuning, and inference settings are not adequately documented. Table 1's SD measures variation across tasks rather than uncertainty across runs or folds, yet small differences support claims about model scaling and architecture. Sample counts also conflict between Figure 3 and Table 3, including house-price and violent-crime totals. These unresolved issues make the current benchmark less reliable than required for acceptance at a top-tier venue.
